title: KV cache architecture & eviction troubleshoot - Helix Security (Deep Dive)
summary: Deep dive into KV cache eviction/paging and prefix reuse. Customer seeing intermittent token-level latency spikes and KV cache thrashing when sessions exceed ~80k tokens; discussion covered cache sizing, eviction policies, prefix reuse best practices, streaming impacts, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run targeted repro with trace logs and share kernel-level latency histograms. Next: SE to provide reproducer script + perf flags; customer to share anonymized logs and sample long-context prompts.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we scheduled an hour for a KV cache deep-dive, I think Maya will drive the technical bits.
[00:06] Maya Chen: hi all, thanks for making time. Can you confirm you're seeing eviction related high p99 token latency?
[00:12] Carlos Rivera: yeah, over the last month we've noticed a few customer sessions that go very long, like 70k-140k tokens, and then all of a sudden latency jumps from 20-40ms per token to 300-600ms for bursts.
[00:21] Priya Nair: it's intermittent, often after certain prompt patterns, seems correlated with prefix reuse but not 100%.
[00:28] Maya Chen: okay, that sounds like partial KV cache thrash or paging to disk. quick clarification: are you using Redwood Dedicated or on-prem?
[00:35] Liam O'Connor: we're on your private deployment inside our VPC, on-prem stack at the edge — so kernel-level metrics are accessible but we have network egress restrictions.
[00:44] Jordan Patel: thanks, that helps. two big knobs: cache size (per-GPU KV capacity) and eviction policy (LRU-ish by default), also page-to-disk behaviour if using swap or our optional p2 paging ext.
[00:54] Carlos Rivera: we haven't changed defaults. curious about prefix reuse — we reuse a system prompt across sessions plus a user history chunk; sometimes multiple different users share near-identical prefix which we think might cause collisions?
[01:05] Maya Chen: prefix reuse shouldn't cause collisions unless the hash/windowing changes; our runtime keys off sequence ID + position, but similar prefixes can increase effective cache pressure because the kv entries overlap, leading to less unique cache per active session.
[01:20] Priya Nair: is there a way to pin prefixes or promote them so they're not evicted?
[01:24] Maya Chen: not by default; we can mark hot prefixes as pinned in Dedicated via config, in Private there's a flag we can enable. pinning increases memory footprint obviously.
[01:33] Liam O'Connor: what's the tradeoff vs batching? We use streaming token-by-token and small batch sizes to hit low latency.
[01:40] Maya Chen: streaming reduces batching opportunities, which increases per-token overhead. However, KV cache is independent; even with streaming, a stable KV cache reduces redundant compute. But if your batch sizes are tiny and you have many active distinct contexts, the working set grows.
[01:52] Jordan Patel: quick note: quantization can change memory usage per key and also slightly alter cache layout — 4-bit vs 8-bit models differ. what model variant are you running?
[01:59] Carlos Rivera: custom 13B tuned model, quantized to 4-bit for throughput.
[02:03] Maya Chen: 4-bit will reduce per-kv entry size but can increase compute variability on GPUs if kernels fall back to different codepaths; that may surface as jitter.
[02:12] Priya Nair: we saw some spikes that aligned with garbage-collection-like events in our nodes, could that be kernel fallback?
[02:19] Maya Chen: possibly — when sequence lengths vary suddenly the runtime may switch attention kernels or memory paths; that can invite short stalls while compilation/caching happens. We can enable warm-up runs to avoid on-the-fly kernel selection.
[02:29] Carlos Rivera: you mentioned paging — does Redwood ever page KV to disk in Private? we thought everything was in GPU+host memory.
[02:36] Maya Chen: by default we keep KV in GPU memory and host pinned memory; paging to disk only occurs if host memory limits are hit or if admins enabled the swap/paging extension. Some customers enable a disk-backed spill to preserve sessions, but that adds big latency when spilled back.
[02:49] Liam O'Connor: hmm we don't have swap enabled. what logs should we collect to prove it's eviction not something else?
[02:55] Maya Chen: good question — we want per-GPU kv_utilization, eviction events, kernel-switch trace, and per-token latency histograms. For Private we'll provide a small agent command to collect ring-buffer traces and the runtime's eviction counter logs.
[03:07] Jordan Patel: I'll drop the reproducer script and perf flags after the call.
[03:11] Carlos Rivera: awesome. a concrete example: session id abc-1234, starts fine for 50k tokens then at ~52k we see large 95/99 jumps; we can share anonymized logs for that ID.
[03:22] Maya Chen: perfect, that's exactly what we need. can you also share the exact prompt pattern around that token boundary? sometimes certain long-range attention patterns blow up memory working set.
[03:32] Priya Nair: yes we'll extract that.
[03:35] Maya Chen: some troubleshooting steps: 1) increase KV capacity per GPU (if you have headroom), 2) enable prefix pinning for the most common system prompt, 3) enable warm-up kernel compilation for long sequences, 4) run a reproducer with batching vs streaming toggles to see effect on eviction rate.
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: how much headroom do we need to avoid thrash? is there a rule of thumb?
[03:57] Maya Chen: rough rule: ensure working set < 70% of total KV capacity; working set estimated as avg active sessions * avg live context length * per-token kv-size. we'll help compute that with your metrics.
[04:10] Carlos Rivera: can cache eviction policy be tuned? we saw an LRU-like policy; could we move to segmented LRU or frequency-based?
[04:17] Maya Chen: in Dedicated we support a few policies: LRU, LFU-ish frequency windows, and a tenant-aware weighted policy that favors sessions with higher priority (e.g., premium customers). In Private we can expose those knobs but it requires a restart to change core settings.
[04:31] Jordan Patel: question from our side — do you have tight SLA windows for token p50/p95?
[04:36] Carlos Rivera: p50 ~ 25ms token, p95 < 100ms, p99 maybe up to 200ms acceptable but spikes beyond 300ms are problematic.
[04:45] Priya Nair: we also need auditability — any change to eviction or pinning needs to be logged for compliance.
[04:50] Maya Chen: we have audit logs and RBAC events; changes can be tied to SAML/Sso identity for trace. we'll attach SOC2 docs later.
[04:58] Liam O'Connor: we run in a constrained VPC — will enabling debug agent to collect ring-buffers require more egress than allowed?
[05:05] Maya Chen: agent uploads can be configured to push only to your internal S3; alternatively you can collect locally and share sanitized blobs via the secure channel. We'll provide an offline collection script.
[05:16] Jordan Patel: quick aside: ModelServeX does an aggressive paging approach — we've seen customers complain about disk-spill latencies. worth noting when you benchmark.
[05:24] Carlos Rivera: yeah we benchmarked against them and saw some outliers.
[05:28] Maya Chen: actionable bench to run: replay session with identical timing using our repro harness, toggle cache size/pinning/policy, and toggle streaming vs 8-16 token microbatching. capture per-token latency and eviction counters.
[05:40] Priya Nair: what's microbatching's impact on memory working set?
[05:44] Maya Chen: microbatching slightly increases concurrency which can increase working set but allows for better kernel utilization; overall often reduces average latency at cost of slightly higher peak kv usage.
[05:55] Jordan Patel: let's talk about prefix reuse specifics: if you have many sessions reusing the same system prompt that should actually reduce effective working set because the shared prefix can be cached once and reused across sessions depending on how you shard requests.
[06:07] Priya Nair: but our observation is opposite — when many sessions share it we see thrash.
[06:11] Maya Chen: that implies the runtime may be materializing separate KV entries per session due to differing sequence IDs or positions; possible root cause is how the client attaches session tokens. we should confirm whether you're using conversation_id header or generating distinct session ids per request.
[06:25] Liam O'Connor: we use per-user session IDs but sometimes front-end assigns new ids after reconnects. could that cause duplicate cache entries?
[06:32] Maya Chen: yes reconnect semantics that change session id lead to duplicate cache entries for same prefix; recommend stable session id and reconnect handling that preserves id.
[06:41] Carlos Rivera: good to know. any tooling to detect duplicate prefixes?
[06:45] Maya Chen: our runtime logs can show fingerprint counts for identical prefix hashes; we'll enable that metric in the repro run.
[06:54] Priya Nair: about eviction histograms — we saw periodic peaks every ~90 minutes across nodes. could that be scheduled GC or cron job?
[07:01] Maya Chen: could be node-level maintenance, or a background compaction job in your cluster. ask infra to check cronjobs and Kubernetes cronjobs (if using EKS). Also check for nightly backup windows that spike IO.
[07:14] Jordan Patel: Maya, can you walk through an example trace of a typical eviction event? like what counters we should expect to see.
[07:20] Maya Chen: sure: at t0 you have kv_utilization 65%, at t1 you have a sudden influx of new contexts, eviction_counter increments, host_mem_pressure rises, kernel-switch shows fallback to host-path, and per-token latency jumps. If paging is enabled you'll see disk_spill_count increment and large tail latencies. Capture timestamps so we can correlate.
[07:38] Carlos Rivera: we'll pull three example timestamps.
[07:41] Maya Chen: also check GPU nvlink peer stats — if you're sharding across GPUs and the KV references cross GPUs, nvlink saturation can show up as increased latency too.
[07:52] Liam O'Connor: that's relevant, we do cross-GPU sharded sessions. How do we avoid cross-GPU KV thrash?
[07:58] Maya Chen: options: co-locate related contexts on the same GPU via smart routing, or increase local KV capacity to reduce cross-GPU fetches. Smart routing can be enabled in Dedicated and Private with a policy table.
[08:11] Priya Nair: smart routing sounds promising, but does it impact load balancing?
[08:15] Maya Chen: it can — the policy tries to balance latency vs throughput; for a few VIP sessions we prioritize latency. We'll share recommended configs.
[08:24] Jordan Patel: let's move to next steps and artifacts.
[08:27] Maya Chen: I'll attach the repro harness, kernel warm-up flags, and a checklist of runtime flags to probe. Jordan will share the security docs and SOC2 link. We need your anonymized logs and sample prompt around the spike token boundary.
[08:40] Carlos Rivera: timeline: we can get logs and prompt examples in 2 business days, and run an initial repro by EOD next week.
[08:48] Priya Nair: also please include the kernel/hardware histograms so our SREs can correlate with node metrics.
[08:55] Jordan Patel: will do. Anything else from Helix?
[08:58] Liam O'Connor: one more: are there known issues with specific quantization toolchains interacting poorly with our model? we used QAT tooling from third party.
[09:05] Maya Chen: some third-party QAT toolchains can produce tensor layouts that trigger slower kernels; we'll look at your specific artifact but usually re-quantizing with our recommended pipeline helps.
[09:15] Carlos Rivera: thanks team.
[09:17] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a proposed repro run schedule.
[09:22] Jordan Patel: recap — SE reproducer + perf flags (Maya), security docs + SOC2 (Jordan), Helix to provide logs + prompts (Carlos/Priya), schedule follow-up after initial repro.
[09:35] Carlos Rivera: that works. thanks everyone.
[09:39] End of recording.
